0.title: Trembling Love Before a Holy God
0.essay:
Few phrases are repeated in the Bible as often as “the fear of the LORD”, and few are less understood today. It is called “the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 111:10), “a fountain of life” (Proverbs 14:27) and “the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Yet many Christians are unsure what it means.

Two mistakes

Some think the fear of God belongs to the Old Testament and was replaced by love in the New. Others quietly assume it means being afraid that God is waiting to punish them. Many simply never think about it. Scripture’s answer is richer than either mistake. The fear of the Lord is the right response of a creature to the holy, majestic and gracious God. It includes awe at his greatness, reverence for his holiness, a sober awareness that he is the Judge of all, and a deep desire not to grieve him.

In the believer it is not the cringing dread of a slave before a cruel master. It is the trembling love of a child before a Father who is also the King of the universe.

Not left behind

The New Testament does not abolish this fear. The early church grew “walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 9:31). Peter tells believers who call God Father to “conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile” (1 Peter 1:17). And Isaiah said of the Messiah himself, “his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:3).

Why it matters

What we fear shapes everything else. Those who do not fear God end up fearing everything else: people, the future, failure, death. Those who fear God find that this one fear frees them from all the others.

The chapters

What the Fear of the Lord Is; Why We Fear Him: The Holiness of God; Fear and Love Together; The Fear of God and the Fear of Man; Lives Shaped by the Fear of the Lord; and The Fruit and Blessing of Fearing God. The study belongs with Biblical Wisdom, which shows how this fear is the beginning of a wise life.

1.title: What the Fear of the Lord Is
1.essay:
At Mount Sinai the people of Israel saw thunder, lightning and smoke, and heard the trumpet, and “the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off” (Exodus 20:18). They begged Moses to speak to them instead of God. Then Moses said something that sounds at first like a contradiction.

Do not fear, so that you may fear

“Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin” (Exodus 20:20). Moses was distinguishing two kinds of fear. One runs away from God, terrified and hiding. The other stays near to God, humbled and reverent, and keeps a person from sin. The first keeps its distance; the second draws near on God’s terms. God did not want his people to flee from him in panic. He wanted them to know him so truly that they would never take him lightly. The fear he wants produces holiness, not hiding.

Christians have long called these the fear of a slave and the fear of a son. A slave fears punishment and wishes he could escape his master. A son reveres his father, fears displeasing him, and would not want to be anywhere else.

A settled orientation of the heart

The fear of the Lord, then, is not mainly an emotion, though it can include strong feelings. It is a settled orientation of the heart toward God. It means taking him seriously — his greatness, his holiness, his word, his authority and his judgment — and living every part of life before his face. It begins with the simple awareness that God sees: “The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good” (Proverbs 15:3). For the wicked that is terrifying. For the believer it is both warning and comfort: no sin is hidden, and no faithfulness is overlooked, no tear unseen, no prayer unheard. Living before God’s eyes is the root of integrity.

It is so central that it can stand for true religion as a whole. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7): a right relationship with God is the foundation of everything else.

Fear and love together

And it always leads to obedience. Moses summed up God’s whole requirement like this: “to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 10:12). Notice that love is in the list. These are not five separate duties but five sides of one life lived toward God. To fear God is to love him with reverence; to love God is to fear him with delight. Fear and love grow from the same root, which is a true knowledge of who God is.

The root of sin, and a gift of grace

When Paul sums up fallen humanity in Romans 3, after a long list of sins of the tongue, the hands and the feet, he names the root: “There is no fear of God before their eyes” (Romans 3:18). People sin freely because they do not take God seriously. They live as though he were absent, or harmless, or would never judge. People who do not fear God will eventually do anything.

But the right fear of God is not something we manufacture. In the new covenant God promises, “I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me” (Jeremiah 32:40). He plants it in his people, and it keeps them from falling away. Often the beginning of salvation is the moment someone first truly fears God, and then discovers the mercy that the fearful need.

Who then is this?

When Jesus calmed the storm, the disciples had been terrified of the wind and the waves. But when the storm stopped, “they were filled with great fear and said to one another, ‘Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?’” (Mark 4:41). Their fear did not disappear when the danger passed. It increased, and it changed direction: from the storm to the one who commands storms.

A man is alone in a hotel room on a business trip, with a laptop and no one to see what he watches. What keeps him pure? Not the fear of being caught, since no one will know. Only the knowledge that God sees, and that sin would grieve the Father who loves him. Like Joseph, he asks, “How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9).

Here is a simple test. When you are tempted to do wrong in secret, what is your question? If it is only, “Will anyone find out?”, the fear of God is weak in you. If it is, “What will this mean before God?”, it is growing.

For reflection

Before this study, what did you think “the fear of the Lord” meant, and where did that idea come from? What is the difference between the fear that kept Israel far off and the fear Moses wanted them to have? In what situations do you most often forget that God sees you?

2.title: Why We Fear Him: The Holiness of God
2.essay:
We fear God because of who he is. “In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1).

Woe is me

A long and prosperous reign had ended, and the nation’s future was uncertain. Isaiah went into the temple and saw the true King, still on his throne. Seraphim, creatures who had never sinned, covered their faces and their feet and called to one another, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!” (Isaiah 6:3). The doorposts shook and smoke filled the house. And Isaiah, perhaps the most righteous man in Jerusalem, cried out, “Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5).

Before he saw God, Isaiah could pronounce woes on others. When he saw God, he pronounced one on himself. That is what happens when a sinner sees the holiness of God: every excuse disappears. Real encounters with God’s holiness always humble. Anyone who claims to have seen God and comes away proud has not seen him.

Creator and Judge

God’s holiness means that he is utterly set apart: above and beyond everything he has made, and perfectly pure, without the smallest trace of evil. He is the Creator, and we are creatures. “Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him!” (Psalm 33:8). Every human being owes him reverence simply because he made us.

He is also the Judge, and we will give account. Jesus, who welcomed sinners, also warned, “Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matthew 10:28). Yet in the next breath he spoke of the same God: not a sparrow falls without your Father, the hairs of your head are numbered — “Fear not, therefore” (Matthew 10:31). The God to be feared above all is the God who cares for his children in every detail. Those who fear him need fear nothing else. That is the logic of this whole study in a single passage.

Paul, the apostle of grace, lived in the awareness that “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). For believers this is not a judgment that decides salvation, which is secure in Christ, but an assessment of how we have lived as his servants. It made Paul earnest: “Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others” (2 Corinthians 5:11). The fear of the Lord does not make Christians timid. It makes them urgent, faithful and bold.

Not an Old Testament idea

Hebrews contrasts Mount Sinai, with its fire and darkness, with Mount Zion, where Christians have come by grace. You might expect the writer to say that the fear of Sinai is gone. Instead he says that because our privilege is greater, our reverence must be deeper: “let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29). God has not changed. Grace does not make him tame. It makes it possible for sinners to approach the fire and not be destroyed. “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

The fear of the Redeemer

Strikingly, Scripture also says we fear God because of his grace. Peter tells believers to live in fear, “knowing that you were ransomed … with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). The price of our redemption shows how seriously God takes sin and how much he has given. Those who understand the cross will never treat God lightly. Isaiah’s woe was followed at once by a burning coal from the altar and the words, “your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for” (Isaiah 6:7).

Our age has largely lost the sense of God’s weight and majesty. He is often spoken of as a friendly helper or a therapist. He is kind beyond words, but he is never small. Only when we see how holy he is do we begin to understand how amazing his grace is.

Holiness seen

When Peter saw the miraculous catch of fish, he did not shout for joy. He fell at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). Like Isaiah, he saw holiness and saw himself. And like Isaiah, he was not sent away but called: from now on he would catch men.

When Ananias and Sapphira lied to the Holy Spirit and fell dead, “great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things” (Acts 5:11). God was teaching the new covenant community that grace does not make him less holy.

Joyful reverence

One church service is full of energy and noise, but almost nothing in it suggests that the people are standing before a holy God. Another is reverent but cold. Neither is what Scripture describes. “I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you” (Psalm 5:7). “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). Joyful reverence and reverent joy belong together, in a congregation and in a single heart.

For reflection

Read Isaiah 6:1–8. What moved Isaiah from “Woe is me” to “Here I am! Send me”? In what ways does our culture, and sometimes the church, make God seem small? How does the cross deepen, rather than remove, your reverence for God? Does your worship reflect both joy and reverence?

3.title: Fear and Love Together
3.essay:
Many Christians feel a tension here. John writes, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment” (1 John 4:18). Paul says we “did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear” (Romans 8:15). Yet the same New Testament tells believers to fear God. How do these fit together?

The fear that love casts out

The answer is in John’s own explanation: the fear that love casts out is the fear that “has to do with punishment”. John is writing about confidence on the day of judgment (1 John 4:17). A believer in Christ need not fear God’s condemnation, because Christ has borne it. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). The terror of the guilty before the Judge is gone. What remains, and grows, is the reverent awe of a child before a holy Father.

Paul contrasts the spirit of slavery with “the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). The Christian life is not lived in the anxious fear of a slave who never knows if he has done enough. It is lived as sons and daughters, secure in the Father’s house. Yet a good father is still honoured. Adoption does not remove reverence. It changes it from dread into love. We call him Father, and we remember that he “judges impartially according to each one’s deeds” (1 Peter 1:17). Both truths keep us humble and secure.

Forgiveness that makes us tremble

Scripture goes further: grace produces the right kind of fear. Psalm 130 asks the worst question there is — if God kept a record of every sin, who could stand? — and then gives the great answer: “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). That is surprising. We might expect forgiveness to make people careless. But forgiveness understood rightly makes a person tremble with grateful wonder. It shows us a God holy enough to see every sin and merciful enough to remove it. People who think God overlooks sin easily do not fear him. People who know what forgiveness cost do.

Those he draws near

The Psalms join fear and love constantly. “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13). Three times in that psalm God’s love is promised to those who fear him (Psalm 103:11, 13, 17): his steadfast love as high as the heavens, our sins removed as far as the east is from the west. “The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him” (Psalm 25:14). “The LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love” (Psalm 147:11). Mary sang, “his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation” (Luke 1:50).

So the fear of the Lord is not distance from God. It is the reverent closeness of those who know him best. It is not a barrier to grace but the posture in which grace is received.

Fear grows with love

In human relationships, the more we love someone, the more we fear to hurt them. A child who loves a good father fears grieving him far more than he fears punishment. So it is with God. Mature Christians do not fear God less than new believers; they fear him more, and love him more, at the same time.

Some worry that taking God’s holiness seriously will rob them of assurance. The opposite is true. Assurance rests on Christ’s finished work, not on our feelings. And it is those who are secure in his love who can most freely stand in awe of his holiness without being crushed by it.

Three people

When Abraham was ready to offer Isaac, the angel said, “for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me” (Genesis 22:12). Abraham’s fear was not terror. It was a love for God greater than his love for the son he had waited for, and a trust that God would provide.

A young Christian who grew up in a harsh home finds the idea of fearing God frightening. She hears it as being afraid of a father who might explode. She needs to hear both halves of the truth. The punishing fear is gone for those in Christ: God is not an angry father waiting to strike. And the God who loves her is so holy, so great and so good that the right response is awe, worship and a desire never to grieve him.

An older believer, after decades of walking with God, says that the more she knows him, the more she trembles at his greatness and the more she rests in his love. That is not a contradiction. It is maturity.

For reflection

How would you explain to a friend the difference between the fear that love casts out and the fear believers are called to? Read Psalm 130: why does forgiveness lead to fearing God rather than taking him lightly? Does your own faith lean more toward fear without love, or love without reverence?

4.title: The Fear of God and the Fear of Man
4.essay:
Everyone fears something. The question is not whether we will fear, but what. And Scripture teaches that the fear of God and the fear of man are rivals: whichever is stronger will rule us.

A snare

“The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). A snare is a hidden trap that catches an animal by the foot and holds it fast. The fear of man works like that. It rarely looks dangerous. It looks like being nice, keeping the peace or being sensible. But it catches us and holds us, until we cannot do what is right because we are afraid of what others will think.

It shows itself in people-pleasing, a craving for approval, dread of criticism, compromise to avoid conflict, silence when we should speak, and lies to protect our image. It can rule a teenager desperate to fit in, a pastor afraid of his congregation, an employee afraid for her job, or a parent afraid of a child’s displeasure. Paul felt its pull and refused it: “For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? … If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). Every Christian faces that choice, often many times a day.

Fear the right one

God’s answer is not to tell us to stop fearing altogether, but to fear the right one. When Judah was in a panic over a military alliance against it, God told Isaiah not to join the national mood: “do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread” (Isaiah 8:12–13). Every generation has its crowd fears — political, economic or cultural — and Christians are tempted to share them. This passage calls us to a different centre. Peter later applies it to Christians facing persecution (1 Peter 3:14–15).

Jesus said the same to the disciples he called his friends: “do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear” (Luke 12:4–5). He was not threatening them; he was protecting them. People can kill the body, and that is all. God has authority over eternity. And in the next breath Jesus spoke of sparrows and the hairs of your head (Luke 12:6–7). The God to be feared is the Father who cares.

What we fear, we serve

Fear is a form of worship. Whatever we fear most, we will obey. If we fear people most, we will do what pleases them; if we fear God most, we will do what pleases him, even when people object.

So the fear of man is not cured mainly by self-esteem or confidence. It is cured by a bigger God. When God is great in our eyes, people shrink to their proper size. They are still to be loved and served, but they are no longer our masters. And when we know we are fully accepted in Christ, we no longer need others’ approval to feel secure.

This freedom does not make Christians careless about people. It frees us to love them truly: to tell them hard truths, to serve them without needing their thanks, and to forgive them when they reject us. People-pleasers cannot really love, because they are always protecting themselves. The man who fears the Lord in the first verse of Psalm 112 is the man in verse 7 who “is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD” (Psalm 112:7). The fear of God is the source of Christian courage.

The midwives and the governor

Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy. “But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live” (Exodus 1:17). Scripture records their names, Shiphrah and Puah (Exodus 1:15), while Pharaoh’s is not given. They had no army, no position and no guarantee of protection. They simply feared God more than the king — and “because the midwives feared God, he gave them families” (Exodus 1:21). The fear of the Lord is not only a private feeling. It shapes courageous action in the public world.

When Nehemiah became governor, the officials before him had taxed the people heavily and let their servants lord it over them. Nehemiah said, “But I did not do so, because of the fear of God” (Nehemiah 5:15). It governed how he used power and money.

In our day

A teenager’s friends are mocking another student online. Joining in would make him popular; refusing will make him a target. Fearing God, he refuses, and quietly sends the victim a kind message.

A pastor knows a passage will offend some influential members. The fear of man says, “Skip it.” The fear of God says, “Preach it faithfully, with love.” He preaches it, and trusts God with the consequences.

An employee is pressured by her manager to falsify figures. Fearing God more than her boss, she refuses respectfully, and is ready to accept the cost.

For reflection

Where do you see the fear of man most in your life: approval, criticism, conflict, reputation? What fears does the crowd around you share, and how should fearing God reshape them? Think of a time the fear of man kept you silent. What would the fear of God have led you to do?

5.title: Lives Shaped by the Fear of the Lord
5.essay:
Scripture does not only teach the fear of the Lord. It shows what it looks like in real lives. Again and again the Bible describes its heroes simply as people who feared God.

Job and Joseph

Job is introduced as a man who “was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil” (Job 1:1), and God himself repeats the description (Job 1:8). The fear of God sits at the centre of his character and shows itself in turning from evil. The rest of the book tests whether Job feared God only because God blessed him (Job 1:9). Through grief, sickness and confusion, his fear of God survived, even when he did not understand God’s ways. True fear of God is not a reward for blessing. It continues when blessing is taken away.

Joseph refused the advances of Potiphar’s wife because the sin would be against God (Genesis 39:9). Years later, as ruler of Egypt, he steadied his frightened brothers with the words, “for I fear God” (Genesis 42:18). His fear of God made him trustworthy in power.

Obadiah in Ahab’s palace

Ahab and Jezebel were among the most wicked rulers in Israel’s history, and Obadiah managed their household. Yet the text says plainly that “Obadiah feared the LORD greatly” (1 Kings 18:3). When Jezebel was killing the prophets, he hid a hundred of them in caves and fed them. He had “feared the LORD from my youth” (1 Kings 18:12). He did not need to leave his job to be faithful; he used his position to protect God’s people. Some believers are called to leave corrupt situations; others, like Obadiah, are placed there by God. The fear of the Lord gives wisdom to know which, and courage to act.

A Christian civil servant today works in a department whose policies often oppose Christian convictions. She does not quit in protest, and she does not blend in. She does excellent work, quietly protects colleagues who are treated unfairly, and refuses to take part in anything dishonest. Like Obadiah, she fears the Lord greatly in a hostile place.

Cornelius

Cornelius was a centurion in the occupying Roman army, a Gentile and an outsider to Israel. Yet Luke describes him as “a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God” (Acts 10:2). God answered him by sending Peter with the gospel, and he became one of the first Gentile converts. Fearing God was not the end of his story but the beginning. The fear of the Lord always points beyond itself to the Saviour.

God often prepares hearts before he sends the messenger. A businessman who is not yet a Christian is generous, prays and leads his family in respect for God. A Christian colleague, seeing his openness, invites him to read the Gospel of John together.

Jonah

Even while running from God, Jonah could say, “I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land” (Jonah 1:9). The irony is sharp. The pagan sailors, seeing God’s power in the storm, “feared the LORD exceedingly” (Jonah 1:16), while the prophet who confessed the fear of the Lord was fleeing from him. Confessing it with our lips is not the same as living it. A church member may speak fluently about reverence for God while nursing bitterness and refusing God’s call to forgive. The fear of the Lord is proved by obedience, not vocabulary.

The one who feared perfectly

Isaiah foretold that the Spirit would rest on the Messiah as “the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2), and that “his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:3). Hebrews lets us see into Gethsemane: “Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence” (Hebrews 5:7). He did not demand; he submitted. His prayer was heard, not by escaping death but by being raised from it. Our fear of God is weak and mixed. His was complete, and we are accepted in him.

A church that fears God

The early church was marked by both fear and comfort: “walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied” (Acts 9:31). Growth in holiness flows from the same source: “let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7:1). And Paul tells believers to “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12–13). The trembling is not fear of losing salvation, but awe that the almighty God is at work within us.

For reflection

Which of these — Job, Joseph, Obadiah, Cornelius — best shows what the fear of the Lord looks like for you now? Where are you called to fear God in a place that does not? Where might your words about God be ahead of your obedience? How does Jesus’ perfect reverence encourage you when your own is weak?

6.title: The Fruit and Blessing of Fearing God
6.essay:
The fear of the Lord is not a gloomy burden. Scripture describes it again and again as the path to life, joy and security. “The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death” (Proverbs 14:27).

A fortress and a fountain

Proverbs puts two pictures side by side. The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, and it is a fortress: “In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge” (Proverbs 14:26). Fear and confidence are not opposites here. The person who fears God is the most secure person in the world, because the one they fear is also their refuge. And the blessing passes down. A home shaped by the fear of God is a safe place to grow up. “The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied” (Proverbs 19:23).

What God promises

Those who fear God are promised his friendship: “The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him” (Psalm 25:14). That is close, confidential fellowship, the kind kept for trusted friends. The holy God, before whom angels cover their faces, draws near in friendship to those who fear him. Reverence does not keep God at a distance; it is the way into his closest fellowship.

They are promised his provision — “Oh, fear the LORD, you his saints, for those who fear him have no lack!” (Psalm 34:9) — and his stored-up goodness: “Oh, how abundant is your goodness, which you have stored up for those who fear you” (Psalm 31:19).

These are not wages earned. They are the fruit of a right relationship with God, which is itself his gift. And they are proverbs, not guarantees: as the Biblical Wisdom study explains, they describe how God’s world normally works. God-fearing people still suffer, as Job did. But in every circumstance they have the deeper blessings: God’s presence, his friendship and an eternal inheritance.

What it makes of us

The fear of the Lord also shapes character. “The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil” (Proverbs 8:13). It makes us humble, honest and pure. It frees us from envy: “Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day” (Proverbs 23:17). And it makes ordinary life rich: “Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it” (Proverbs 15:16).

A couple facing financial hardship decide to keep giving to their church and to the poor, trusting God’s care. They do not become wealthy. But they find that a little with the fear of the Lord is richer than they imagined: contentment, peace in their home, and children who learn that God can be trusted.

Remembered by God

In Malachi’s day, when many had grown cynical, “those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD and esteemed his name” (Malachi 3:16). God notices those who fear him, even when the world does not. A small group meets each week to read Scripture and encourage one another. The world takes no notice. God does, and writes their names in his book.

How it grows

We grow in the fear of the Lord by looking at God: as we read his word, which reveals his holiness and grace; as we worship with his people; as we pray with reverence; as we remember the cross; and as we keep the coming judgment and the coming glory before our eyes. After the Red Sea, “the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses” (Exodus 14:31), and then they sang. Fear and faith grew together as they saw what God had done.

David prayed, “unite my heart to fear your name” (Psalm 86:11). Our hearts are divided. Part of us fears God, and part fears people, failure, loss or the future. David asks God to gather those scattered loyalties into one undivided reverence. It is a prayer God loves to answer, because he has promised to put his fear in our hearts.

This week, read Isaiah 6 or Revelation 4 slowly. Begin prayer by adoring God before asking for anything. Before a decision, ask, “What would honour God as holy here?” At the end of each day, remember one way God showed his greatness and one way he showed his mercy.

The whole duty, and the end

After all the searching of Ecclesiastes, this is the conclusion: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13). The fear of God is not one virtue among many. It is the shape of a life lived rightly before him.

And one day all creation will join in. Those who have conquered by the blood of the Lamb sing, “Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you” (Revelation 15:4). For the redeemed, that fear will be pure joy: the awe of beholding the holy God for ever. To fear him now is to begin the life of heaven on earth.

For reflection

Which promise to those who fear God means the most to you, and why? How does Malachi 3:16–18 encourage you? Pray Psalm 86:11 for yourself: where is your heart divided between fearing God and fearing something else? Choose one habit to help you grow in the fear of the Lord this week.
